sections.title: Rational choice
sections.keyIdea: Consumers are assumed to compare marginal benefit with marginal cost and choose the option with the greatest net gain.

body.text: The assumption of rationality says consumers aim to maximise **utility** and firms aim to maximise profit.

steps: Compare marginal benefit and marginal cost

realExample.text: A shopper in Kuala Lumpur comparing two phone plans weighs the extra data against the extra monthly cost before choosing.

sections.misconception: Students often write that rational means selfish. It means consistent: choosing the option with the greatest net benefit. Write: rational consumers weigh marginal benefit against marginal cost.
sections.examMatters: A 4-mark Explain needs the assumption stated and one reason consumers may not meet it.

recall.prompt: Put the rational decision-making process in order, from first step to last:
correctOrder: Compare marginal benefit against marginal cost
Choose the option with the greatest net benefit
why: You cannot compare what you have not listed
Marginal benefit against marginal cost is the comparison a rational agent makes
The option with the greatest net benefit is the rational choice

sections.title: Why consumers may not maximise utility
sections.keyIdea: Herding, habit, inertia, weak computation, the need to feel valued and framing all pull consumers away from the rational choice.

body.text: Herding is following other people. Habitual behaviour repeats past choices. Inertia is not switching even when a better option exists. Framing means the same choice looks different when presented differently.

realExample.text: Singapore commuters keep the same kopi order for years even when a cheaper stall opens next door: habit and inertia, not calculation.

sections.misconception: Students think inertia means laziness. It means the cost of switching, including effort, is felt more than the gain. Write: inertia keeps consumers on a worse deal because switching feels costly.
sections.examMatters: Name the behaviour and explain why it stops utility being maximised.

content.title: The demand curve
takeaway: Price changes move along the curve
Diminishing marginal utility explains the slope

sections.title: Movements and shifts
sections.keyIdea: A change in the good's own price moves along the demand curve; a change in any other factor shifts the whole curve.

body.text: Own price causes a **movement**. Income, tastes, substitutes and complements cause a **shift**.

realExample.text: When Hong Kong incomes rose in 2023, demand for premium phones shifted right at every price.

sections.misconception: Students say a price rise shifts demand left. It causes a movement along the curve. Write: a shift needs a non-price factor.
sections.examMatters: The distinction is worth a mark on its own in a 4-mark Explain.

recall.prompt: Order the steps when incomes rise, from cause to effect:
correctOrder: Demand for normal goods shifts right
why: A rise in real income is the trigger
A normal good is one whose demand rises with income, so its demand curve shifts right
A rightward shift raises both equilibrium price and quantity

sections.title: Price elasticity of demand
sections.keyIdea: PED measures how much quantity demanded responds to a change in price.

body.text: PED is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price.

realExample.text: Fuel demand in Pakistan changed little when prices rose sharply in 2022, a sign of inelastic demand.

sections.misconception: Students treat PED as positive. It is negative for normal goods; the sign is conventionally dropped. Write: PED = %ΔQd ÷ %ΔP.
sections.examMatters: Show the formula and interpret the number.

content.title: Income and cross elasticity
takeaway: YED sign tells normal from inferior
XED sign tells substitutes from complements
Both are ratios of percentage changes

sections.title: Income elasticity
sections.keyIdea: YED measures how quantity demanded responds to a change in income; positive for normal goods, negative for inferior goods.

body.text: A positive YED marks a normal good; a negative YED marks an inferior good.

realExample.text: Bus travel in Jakarta fell as incomes rose and riders switched to motorbikes: an inferior good.

sections.misconception: Students call inferior goods low quality. Inferior describes the income response, not the product. Write: demand falls as income rises.
sections.examMatters: State the sign and what it implies.

recall.prompt: Order the reasoning from cause to effect:
correctOrder: Consumers switch away from inferior goods
why: A rise in income is the trigger
An inferior good is one consumers trade up from as they can afford better
Fewer buyers means demand for those goods falls

content.title: Elasticity and revenue
takeaway: Inelastic demand: raise price, raise revenue
Elastic demand: cut price, raise revenue

sections.title: PED and total revenue
sections.keyIdea: When demand is price inelastic a price rise raises total revenue; when it is elastic a price rise lowers it.

body.text: Total revenue is price times quantity. The direction it moves after a price change depends on PED.

realExample.text: Ticket prices for a sold-out K-pop tour rose 20% and revenue rose, because demand was inelastic.

sections.misconception: Students think higher prices always mean more revenue. Only with inelastic demand. Write: compare the percentage changes.
sections.examMatters: A calculation with the formula earns the quantitative marks.

template: If demand is price ___, a price rise raises total revenue

quiz.question: Which of these is a reason a consumer may not maximise utility?
quiz.explanation: Inertia keeps a consumer on an existing choice even when a better one exists.

quiz.question: A rise in the price of a good causes:
options: A shift of the demand curve left
A movement along the demand curve
A shift of the demand curve right
quiz.explanation: Own price changes cause movements; other factors cause shifts.

quiz.question: Which factor shifts the demand curve for a normal good to the right?
options: A fall in its own price
A rise in its own price
A fall in the price of a complement's substitute
quiz.explanation: Income is a non-price factor, so it shifts the curve.

quiz.question: A good with a negative income elasticity of demand is:
If PED is 0.4 and price rises by 10%, quantity demanded falls by:
Which describes diminishing marginal utility?
options: Each extra unit adds less satisfaction
Each extra unit adds more satisfaction
Total utility falls from the first unit
quiz.explanation: Extra satisfaction falls as consumption rises.

quiz.question: A positive cross elasticity of demand between two goods means they are:
quiz.explanation: A rise in one price raises demand for the other.

quiz.question: Which is most likely to have price inelastic demand?
quiz.explanation: Few substitutes and a small share of spending.

quiz.question: A complement to a good is one whose:
options: Price rise raises demand for the good
Price rise lowers demand for it
quiz.explanation: A rise in a complement's price lowers demand for the good.

quiz.question: Ceteris paribus means:
Which of these is a substitute for tea?
Which term means the overall satisfaction gained from all units of a good consumed?
Which term means the extra satisfaction from one more unit?
quiz.explanation: The extra satisfaction from one more unit.
